data.title: New to The Street Show 775 Premieres Tonight on Bloomberg Television Across the United States, Latin America, MENA and Southeast Asia, Featuring American Fusion, HPB, T-REX Acquisition Corp. and SyncMeOn
data.description:
NEW YORK CITY, NY / ACCESS Newswire / October 10, 2026 / New to The Street, the financial-media platform for public companies, pre-IPO companies and entrepreneurs, today announced that Show 775 will premiere tonight at 6:30 p.m. ET on Bloomberg Television as sponsored programming. The episode will reach business audiences across four global regions: the United States, Latin America, the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) and Southeast Asia.

Hosted by Jane King and opening from the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, Show 775 features executive interviews with Brent Nelson, Executive Chairman of American Fusion Inc. (OTCQB:AMFN); Dr. Sebastian Heinz, Chief Executive Officer of HPB (High Performance Battery); David McPhail, Chief Executive Officer of T-REX Acquisition Corp. (OTCQB:TRXA); and Alex Mouravieff, CEO and Founder of SyncMeOn.

The broadcast also carries television commercials from BioVie Inc. (NASDAQ:BIVI), Lantern Pharma Inc. (NASDAQ:LTRN), Big Sky Industrial (NASDAQ:BSIN) and FreeCast (CAST).

After the broadcast, every segment will be distributed across the largest YouTube ecosystem in the public-company space, the New to The Street TV and NewsOut channels, with more than 6.6 million combined subscribers.

"Show 775 puts four companies working on some of the biggest questions in the market, from where the next generation of power comes from to how it is stored, in front of investors in four global regions in a single half hour," said Vince Caruso, Co-Founder and CEO of New to The Street. "Fusion energy, solid-state batteries, the infrastructure behind digital assets and smarter restaurant supply chains are the kinds of stories that travel across borders. That is what our global Bloomberg footprint is built to deliver: No politics. No current events. Only Opportunities to Consider™."

Inside Show 775

American Fusion Inc. (OTCQB:AMFN): The Texatron™ Fusion Engine™ and the Power Demands of the AI Era
Executive Chairman Brent Nelson discusses the company's Texatron™ Fusion Engine™, an aneutronic fusion platform designed for modular, infrastructure-grade deployment across industrial, commercial, defense and grid-constrained applications. The conversation covers the company's growing intellectual-property portfolio, ongoing Texatron™ testing and validation, and preparations for a potential uplisting from OTCQB to a national securities exchange, as outlined in the company's September 22, 2026 corporate update. Learn more at www.americanfusionenergy.com.

HPB (High Performance Battery): A Non-Flammable, Long-Life Solid-State Battery
Dr. Sebastian Heinz joins Jane King to discuss the HPB Solid-State Battery, a non-flammable, cobalt-free cell that HPB reports has completed more than 12,500 full charge cycles, roughly ten times a conventional lithium-ion battery under comparable conditions. Dr. Heinz explains HPB's licensing model, in which manufacturers build and run production locally rather than HPB constructing its own gigafactories, and why long-duration stationary storage, including the fast-growing power needs of data centers, is a natural fit for the technology. Learn more at www.highperformancebattery.ch.

T-REX Acquisition Corp. (OTCQB:TRXA): Vertically Integrated Digital-Asset Infrastructure
Chief Executive Officer David McPhail presents T-REX's vertically integrated digital-asset business, which spans proprietary Bitcoin mining, data-center hosting and co-location services, crypto-mining container fabrication and mining-management software. Learn more at www.t-rexminingsolutions.com.

SyncMeOn: Bringing Price Transparency to Restaurant Procurement
CEO and Founder Alex Mouravieff introduces SyncMeOn, an open marketplace and software platform that connects restaurants with food suppliers in real time. Mouravieff explains how operators can compare what they pay against available market pricing, discover new suppliers and connect directly in a more transparent procurement environment. Learn more at www.syncmeon.com.

Featured Commercials

  • BioVie Inc. (NASDAQ:BIVI) - clinical-stage company developing investigational therapies for neurological and neurodegenerative disorders
  • Lantern Pharma Inc. (NASDAQ:LTRN) - AI-driven oncology company, featuring its withZETA.ai research platform for rare cancers
  • Big Sky Industrial (NASDAQ:BSIN) - strategic energy infrastructure, including the Big Sky Carbon Hub, a facility designed to extract a single gas stream to sell high-value helium
  • FreeCast (CAST) - a streaming platform addressing fragmentation across today's leading streaming services

A Four-Region Bloomberg Footprint

Following the launch of Southeast Asia distribution with Show 774 on October 3, 2026, New to The Street now delivers its featured companies to business audiences across the United States, Latin America, MENA and Southeast Asia every week, positioning it as one of the most widely distributed public-company programs on global business television.

How to Watch

  • Bloomberg Television: Tonight, Saturday, October 10, 2026, at 6:30 p.m. ET, with distribution across the United States, Latin America, MENA and Southeast Asia
  • New to The Street TV on YouTube: youtube.com/@NewtoTheStreetTV
  • NewsOut on YouTube: youtube.com/@NewsOutChannel

Now Booking Q1 2027

New to The Street is booking public companies, emerging-growth businesses and companies preparing to enter the public markets for its Q1 2027 global television and digital programming lineup.

Booking contact:
John Battenfield
John@NewtoTheStreet.com

About New to The Street

Founded in 2009, New to The Street is a sponsored and syndicated business television platform serving public companies, emerging-growth businesses and companies aspiring to enter the public markets. Co-founded and led by CEO Vince Caruso, New to The Street combines weekly Bloomberg Television broadcasts across the United States, Latin America, MENA and Southeast Asia with long-form executive interviews, television commercials, earned media, social-media distribution, NewsOut video press-release coverage, accredited-investor events and premium outdoor advertising, including Times Square billboards. Its YouTube ecosystem, the New to The Street TV and NewsOut channels, is the largest in the public-company space, with more than 6.6 million combined subscribers. New to The Street is produced by FMW Media Works LLC. No politics. No current events. Only Opportunities to Consider™.

data.title: AI Made Music Fast. CITY JAM Founder Pat Villaceran Says the Real Asset Is the Artist's Own Sound
data.description:
AI Made Music Fast. CITY JAM Founder Pat Villaceran Says the Real Asset Is the Artist's Own Sound

AI Made Music Fast. CITY JAM Founder Pat Villaceran Says the Real Asset Is the Artist's Own Sound

PR Newswire

NEW YORK, Oct. 10, 2026

As AI music races on speed and volume, CITY JAM's INDUSTRY.AIFF works on what no pipeline can force: drawing original sound out of human creators.

NEW YORK, Oct. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Generative AI has made music fast, and the race in AI music is now about speed and volume. Pat Villaceran, founder of CITY JAM, says that race leaves one input untouched: original sound from human creators. Drawing that sound out of artists is both an art and a science. It is the craft behind INDUSTRY.AIFF, which takes a label's signed-but-unfinished artists to catalog-ready work and carries them through launch.

"When you stack up the progress around AI, it's all about speed, and about getting human creators back on track. That is an art and a science of its own," said Villaceran. "There are blueprints in it. Anyone can copy a blueprint: the roadmap, the pipeline, the scheduling and the workflows. But you cannot force the sound to come out if it has to be an original sound. The creativity is in how you bring out and evoke insights from musicians and creatives, and that is what CREATOR LABS and INDUSTRY.AIFF do. How you do that is the expertise we have at CITY JAM."

In tech terms, the blueprint is the easy part. A release plan can be written down and handed to anyone. Software can run it. The sound, Villaceran says, cannot.

The figures show how fast supply has moved. Luminate's 2025 Year-End Music Report counted 106,000 tracks a day reaching streaming services in 2025, up 7% on 99,000 a day in 2024. In 2025, 120.5 million of 253 million audio tracks had ten streams or fewer. That is almost half.

A growing share of that supply is not made by people. On Deezer, fully AI-generated tracks reached almost 75,000 a day in April 2026, roughly 44% of daily uploads, and passed 50% of new uploads at the June 2026 peak. Yet AI tracks are 1 to 3% of streams on Deezer, and up to 85% of those streams were fraudulent in 2025. On Deezer, the flood is in uploads, not listening.

The CISAC and PMP Strategy study projects that generative AI "could put 24% of Music creators' revenues at risk in 2028." That is a projection.

The US Copyright Office is now asking what that volume costs. Its inquiry into music streaming fraud names, in its Federal Register notice, "the dilution of the royalty revenue pool" as the primary harm, and asks which industry practices may be "inadvertently contributing to streaming fraud." Initial comments are due November 23, 2026, and replies December 21, 2026.

Detection and enforcement sit with regulators and the streaming services. CITY JAM's work sits earlier, in the stretch between signing an artist and a finished record. The royalty pool is diluted by volume without an audience. Fully finished, genuine releases are what the pool is for, and those still depend on an artist finding a sound of their own.

So if speed is no longer the hard part, what is music for? Villaceran's answer is the artist's own sound. It has to be drawn out of the musician. Then the speed AI brings can serve an original sound instead of replacing it.

INDUSTRY.AIFF does this for record labels and artist services companies. It works with their signed artists from unfinished work to catalog-ready releases, and stays with them through launch.

INDUSTRY.AIFF sits within the AI-era accelerator and incubator model for music that Villaceran launched on October 9, 2026, starting with record labels. Artists get the kind of support a startup accelerator gives founders. Education and professional development sit alongside community and live jam sessions. Collaborations and commercial opportunities come with it, and so does technology.

About CITY JAM

CITY JAM is holistic, end-to-end infrastructure for the music industry, built for everyone from independent musicians to record labels and artist services companies. It runs INDUSTRY.AIFF and CREATOR LABS with a global network of experts and producers, including CITY JAM New York. Pat Villaceran founded and leads CITY JAM. She also founded the innovation agency The MooVe, and has built innovation programs for companies and founders in Asia Pacific and the United States as well as in the United Kingdom and Europe. CITY JAM brings that record to music. INDUSTRY.AIFF is CITY JAM's program for record labels and artist services companies, and the name of its weekday letter for music label CEOs. CREATOR LABS is a holistic support system for independent musicians. It is a separate offering and is not part of INDUSTRY.AIFF. CITY JAM is a brand of HINABI PRIVE, INC. For updates, follow CITY JAM on LinkedIn.

Media contact: CITY JAM, press@themoove.co

data.title: Real Estate Expert Mark Williams Explains What to Check Before Buying Land Near Greeneville in HelloNation
data.description:
Real Estate Expert Mark Williams Explains What to Check Before Buying Land Near Greeneville in HelloNation

Real Estate Expert Mark Williams Explains What to Check Before Buying Land Near Greeneville in HelloNation

PR Newswire

GREENEVILLE, Tenn., Oct. 10, 2026

The article outlines key factors that help buyers avoid costly mistakes when purchasing raw land.

GREENEVILLE, Tenn., Oct. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- What should buyers evaluate before purchasing property in Greeneville, Tennessee? A HelloNation article answers this question, featuring insights from Real Estate Expert Mark Williams of Greeneville, Tennessee.

The article explains that buying land differs significantly from purchasing an existing home. Greeneville, Tennessee, buying land involves unique risks, hidden costs, and long-term considerations that can affect usability and overall value. Careful research before closing is presented as essential to avoiding expensive surprises.

Property access is described as the first critical factor to confirm. The article notes that buyers must verify whether legal access is provided by a public road, private road, or easement. Easements may limit how the property can be used or developed, so reviewing official records is important. Walking the land to assess slopes, terrain, and potential obstacles can also reveal additional costs that may arise when improving access.

A land survey is another key component in the evaluation process. The HelloNation article emphasizes the importance of clearly defined boundaries. If an updated land survey is not available, buyers are encouraged to obtain one. Knowing exact property lines helps prevent disputes with neighbors and supports proper planning for buildings, fencing, and other improvements.

Utilities and infrastructure play a major role in determining whether land is practical for its intended use. The article explains that buyers should confirm the availability of electricity, water, sewer, and internet services. In some rural areas near Greeneville, Tennessee, installing utilities can be expensive and time-consuming. Septic suitability and well water access must also be evaluated carefully before moving forward.

Environmental conditions and soil quality are presented as additional factors that can influence long-term plans. The article suggests walking the property after rainfall to observe drainage patterns and identify standing water. Soil quality can affect construction stability, septic installation, and landscaping potential. Flood risk and erosion concerns may also impact insurance costs and overall safety.

Zoning regulations are another important consideration when buying land. Local zoning laws determine whether property can be used for residential, agricultural, or commercial purposes. The article notes that setbacks, conservation easements, and other restrictions may limit development options. Reviewing zoning requirements early in the process helps buyers avoid disappointment after purchase.

Road maintenance responsibilities are also addressed. For properties located on private roads, buyers should understand who is responsible for upkeep and seasonal repairs. Shared maintenance agreements or homeowner obligations may add ongoing expenses. Clarifying these responsibilities helps prevent disputes and unexpected costs.

Financial planning is emphasized throughout the article. While undeveloped property may have a lower purchase price, preparing it for construction often involves additional expenses. Surveys, permits, utility installation, and infrastructure improvements should all be factored into the budget. The article explains that realistic cost estimates help buyers make informed decisions.

Finally, the HelloNation article highlights the value of working with a real estate agent and other local professionals. Experienced guidance can help buyers review property history, zoning details, and development potential. Professional insight reduces the likelihood of costly errors and ensures legal requirements are properly addressed.

In summary, the article underscores that buying land in Greeneville, Tennessee, requires attention to property access, utilities, zoning, soil quality, environmental conditions, and a current land survey. Careful research and thoughtful planning increase the likelihood of a successful purchase and reduce long-term risks.

What to Check Before Buying Land Near Greeneville, Tennessee features insights from Mark Williams, Real Estate Expert of Greeneville, Tennessee, in HelloNation.

HelloNation is America's Good News Network, a premier media platform built on the idea that good news travels faster when real people tell real stories. Through its community-focused publications and innovative "edvertising" approach, HelloNation delivers content that informs, inspires, and spotlights the leaders making a meaningful impact in their communities.

data.title: Compact Gaming Freedom, Precise Performance, Richer Sound: Epomaker HE60 Hall Effect Keyboard
data.description:
NEW YORK CITY, NY / ACCESS Newswire / October 10, 2026 / The Epomaker HE60 combines a compact gaming-focused design with refined sound tuning and responsive performance. Built for players who value speed and experience, it combines precise magnetic switch technology, a carefully tuned acoustic structure, and versatile connectivity in a space-saving 60% layout.

Compact 60% Design Built for Gaming Freedom
The Epomaker HE60 adopts a compact 60% layout that saves valuable desk space while creating more room for mouse movement, making it especially suitable for FPS gamers who rely on wide and fast mouse motions. Despite its smaller footprint, the keyboard delivers a stable, comfortable experience through thoughtful structural design. The two-stage feet, rarely seen on magnetic keyboards, allow users to adjust the typing angle based on their preferred posture, improving comfort during long gaming sessions and everyday use.

Magnetic Precision Engineered for Competitive Play
Equipped with factory-lubed Creamy Jade Hall Effect magnetic switches, the Epomaker HE60 delivers a responsive typing feel with a slightly firm press, strong rebound, and clear feedback. Its adjustable Rapid Trigger with 0.005mm precision allows players to fine-tune key response based on different gaming habits, helping achieve faster reactions and more consistent control during intense gameplay. Advanced features such as DKS and SOCD further expand customization options, allowing users to optimize key behaviors for competitive scenarios. With high-speed input performance supported by both wired and 2.4GHz modes, the HE60 ensures every movement and command is captured quickly and accurately.

Tuned for a Deeper and More Satisfying Thocky Sound
Beyond speed and responsiveness, the Epomaker HE60 focuses on delivering a more refined acoustic experience. The Creamy Jade magnetic switches, tray-mount structure, aluminum positioning plate, and carefully tuned internal filling system work together to create a fuller and more concentrated sound profile. Through its five-layer sound-dampening design, the keyboard reduces unwanted resonance while enhancing sound consistency across every keystroke. The result is a rich, stable, and satisfying Thocky sound experience straight out of the box, without requiring additional modifications.

Flexible Connectivity with a Distinctive Gaming Identity
The Epomaker HE60 supports Bluetooth, 2.4GHz wireless, and USB wired connections, offering flexible switching between gaming setups, workstations, and mobile devices. Both wired and 2.4GHz modes support up to 8000Hz polling for low-latency performance, while the built-in 8000mAh battery provides extended wireless usage despite the higher power demands commonly associated with magnetic keyboards. Available in black and white color options, the HE60 offers different styles to match individual preferences, from a more performance-focused gaming aesthetic to a cleaner desktop setup. Its gaming-inspired ribbon design adds visual character while also making the keyboard easier to carry.

Price and Availability
The Epomaker HE60 is now available on the Epomaker official website, Amazon store, and AliExpress store. The keyboard is available for $59.99 on the official website.

data.title: Flu season is already here. Here's what to know about this year's flu shots.
data.description:
By Jaimy Lee

There are several options for flu shots, including the first mRNA flu vaccine, which was developed by Moderna

There are several options for flu shots this year, including a new mRNA-based flu vaccine developed by Moderna and Sanofi's Fluzone, which is available as a regular shot and as a high-dose version for people over 65.

The flu season has arrived earlier than expected this year.

The rate of flu-related visits to a doctor's office, emergency room or hospital for the week ending Sept. 13 was double what it was last year at the same time, according to Epic Research, which gathers data from hospitals that use Epic for their electronic medical records. That translates to the flu season landing about seven weeks earlier than in 2025 or 2024.

The Epic data, which was published Thursday, show that the flu is hitting states like Alaska, Hawaii, Florida, Louisiana, Mississippi and Texas the hardest. The drugstore chain Walgreens has seen a double-digit jump in sales of cold and flu medications as well as cough drops, according to a report in ABC News.

"For people who are there, I'm telling people: 'Get your flu shot ASAP,'" said Celine Gounder, an infectious-disease doctor and editor at large for public health at KFF Health News. "For everybody else, before the end of the month. We have this expression: Flu before 'boo' for Halloween."

There are several flu shots available this year, including Moderna's (MRNA) mFLUSIVA, a new mRNA-based shot that's approved for Americans who are at least 50 years old. When compared with GSK's (GSK) Fluarix, Moderna's vaccine produced higher antibody titers, according to a small study that evaluated the two vaccines in 75 people in the U.S. and that was recently published in Nature Immunology.

The mFLUSIVA vaccine is more effective than other flu shots, although it comes with more side effects, which are similar to what people experience with Moderna's COVID-19 vaccine.

There are also the standard options available like CSL Seqirus's Fluad, which is approved for older adults; AstraZeneca's (AZN) FluMist, a nasal spray that is approved for children and adults younger than 50; and Sanofi's (FR:SAN) Fluzone, which is available as a regular shot and as a high-dose version that has been cleared for use in people over 65. All available flu shots in the U.S. are trivalent vaccines, meaning they help protect against H1N1, H3N2 and B/Victoria.

This year's flu season may be worsened by a mutation in the H3N2 strain, particularly in people younger than 25, according to Gounder. Flu rates are also rising early in other parts of the Northern Hemisphere, such as Japan and the U.K.

-Jaimy Lee

data.title: 'The pain was excruciating': A friend in her 80s fell down her basement stairs. What could we have done to prevent it?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'She developed pleural effusion - fluid between the lungs and ribs - compressing her lungs and making it hard for her to breathe'

"My aunt had a stairlift installed when severe arthritis made the stairs dangerous." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

I read the letter from the 80-year-old reader who wondered whether he should renovate or downsize ('I have $400,000 in equity': I'm 80. Should I sell my house because of dangerous stairs - or spend thousands renovating?).

Here's a cautionary tale, which your readers may find of interest in light of that story. A friend in her 80s slipped on the stairs to her flooded basement and fell, breaking two posterior ribs and injuring her shoulder.

The pain was excruciating. She developed pleural effusion - fluid between the lungs and ribs - compressing her lungs and making it hard for her to breathe. A chest tube was inserted to drain the fluid.

Her sister traveled from out of state to help, and once my friend can travel, she will convalesce with her family in another state. She faces months of healing and rehabilitation to get back to full health.

My aunt had a stairlift installed for her steep staircase when severe arthritis made the stairs dangerous for her. There are many options for the person in question to consider. It's wise to take dangerous stairs seriously.

Forevery Wary About Stairs

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: My wife never went back to work after raising our kids. Do I have to share my retirement savings 50/50?

People do put stairlifts into basement stairwells, but when cost is an issue, choices need to be made.

Dear Wary,

A stairlift can be a lifesaver for millions of older adults. It can also be expensive.

People do put stairlifts into basement stairwells, but the steeper and narrower space can make them trickier and possibly more expensive to install. Depending on the configuration of the stairs, it may be more practical to install a stairlift on the main staircase, which is often the most heavily used set of stairs in the house. Your friend was unlucky that she took a tumble on those basement stairs. If in doubt about stairs, older people should wait for a friend or family member, but it's also easier to lecture people after the fact.

If you have reduced mobility, stairlifts are an effective way to remain in your house. Government grants, veterans' benefits and local programs can help with the cost. What happened to your friend is an all-too-common occurrence, and Medicare can foot the cost for necessary inpatient rehab, as long as its eligibility requirements are met. A fall can lead to broken bones, and remaining sedentary for weeks or months while recovering can have a domino effect on a senior's health.

There are a couple of understandable reasons older people put off installing a stairlift. They might also hesitate to install a shower chair or add handrails at the front door for all the neighbors to see. These things are an acknowledgement to others and to yourself that you're getting older. And stairlifts, notwithstanding any grants, are not cheap. They can cost anywhere from $5,000 to $15,000 to install, depending on the brand and the stairwell.

Related: 'We lived within our means': I earned $30,000 as a pastor and still retired comfortably. Why don't you tell people that?

Falls can be traumatic and even fatal

For anyone in a similar situation, before deciding to sell a house you love, consider whether relatively modest changes can make it safe enough to remain there - and whether the house can continue to work for you if your mobility declines further. Such changes will vary in cost and might mean adding a stairlift, better lighting, handrails, nonslip surfaces, a safer bathroom or even relocating a bedroom to the main floor.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has some startling statistics. Every year, there are roughly 4.5 million visits to emergency rooms due to elderly people falling, resulting in 3.1 million treated and released and 1.4 million hospitalizations (falls account for 88% of emergency-room visits for hip fractures among older adults). Falls are the most common cause of traumatic brain injuries for older adults and result in around 43,000 fatalities every year.

Falls are the most common cause of traumatic brain injuries for older adults.

Staircases are a flashpoint for accidents in general. More than 1 million people visit ERs each year for stair-related injuries, with young children and older adults more likely to injure themselves this way, according to a study published in the American Journal of Emergency Medicine. Women are injured more often than men. Older adults are also more likely to suffer fractures, while younger children are more likely to sustain head and neck injuries.

As well as broken or uneven steps, weak ankles or knees and inappropriate footwear, a variety of other factors can lead to falls, the CDC says. Those include lower-body weakness; vitamin D deficiency; age-related balance and mobility issues (especially after a period of illness or, say, a pandemic); side effects of prescription drugs like tranquilizers, sedatives or antidepressants; and even some over-the-counter medicines such as antihistamines and sleep aids.

Don't miss: 'We made a bad, bad decision': I learned the hard way how to manage my aging father's money

Psychological and physical independence

And, yes, the desire to do things yourself is understandable, if sometimes regrettable. Why wait for the housekeeper to make that trip to the garden shed for hedge clippers? Why ask someone else to climb a stepladder to reach a cobweb? We all take chances, sometimes without thinking about the cumulative risk. A fall can rob older people of the very independence that they are trying to preserve by carrying out those tasks.

As your friend's experience illustrates, when an older person falls, the effects can be long-lasting, and not just physically. I recently saw an elderly woman fall at a book signing. She tripped backwards over a wooden platform, and I was surprised that she was able to get up, but the biggest surprise was how it affected her emotionally. She had had a fright and could not even deal with the concern and empathy of onlookers.

In addition to the complications your friend endured, a bad fall can lead to loss of mobility and even a possible withdrawal from social situations due to fear of falling again. You may endure a period of time where you cannot put your own clothes, bathe, or even cook or feed yourself. With or without other age-related medical conditions like heart disease, hypertension, frailty or Parkinson's disease, you may experience a psychological as well as a physical spiral.

A stairlift can help preserve your independence, but it's only one part of the solution.

data.title: 'People in the U.S. need to wake up': As a mortgage loan officer, I rejected applications from wealthy couples. Here's why.
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'People in the U.S. need to wake up'

"I would have a blue-collar 'Joe Six-Pack' who made substantially less but saved and saved and saved, and who got the loan he needed for a house." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

This is one of the best letters that I have read in my lifetime (We lived within our means: I earned $30,000 as a pastor and still retired comfortably). I used to be a mortgage loan officer. I would get a couple that each made six figures but would have difficulty qualifying them for the loan amount they wanted because of their consumer-debt load.

Conversely, I would have a blue-collar "Joe Six-Pack" who made substantially less but saved and saved and saved, and who got the loan he needed for a house. People in the U.S. need to wake up and not be compulsive: Quit buying things you really don't need. It's that way with the federal government as well, and based on that, we'd better get real quick or we're going to have a financial crisis that makes the Great Recession of 2008 look like a picnic.

Saver, Not a Spender

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: I'm 77, pay rent and live off Social Security, but I help homeless people. Why are so many people going hungry?

In 2025, credit unions had a denial rate of about 18.5%, significantly lower than both commercial banks and independent mortgage brokers.

Dear Saver,

With the 30-year mortgage rate hitting 7.3%, your letter comes not a moment too soon.

About your time as a mortgage loan officer: I'm sure there were many hardworking people whose applications you hated to have to decline, but I also suspect that you probably remember the applicants who should have looked great on paper - with six-figure-plus incomes, good prospects and steady jobs but, alas, also with lavish spending habits, car loans, student loans (through no fault of their own) and credit-card debt. That last one is a doozy. You're not wrong that millions of wide-eyed and, perhaps, naive homebuyers see their applications rejected every year.

Having a high income, as you rightly point out, is not the same as having financial security or discipline. Likewise, a low income does not mean that you can't retire and enjoy that chapter of your life in comfort. There are four horsemen of the financial apocalypse: income, spending, debt and savings. You can earn $200,000 a year and still be financially fragile if every red cent is committed to credit-card debt and sustaining an extravagant lifestyle, or you can build a financially secure life by living below your means while earning a fraction of that amount.

Be careful about comparing household finances to government finances, even if it's tempting to do so.

A word to the wise: Be careful about comparing household finances to government finances. It's a tempting comparison to make, but you're not comparing apples to apples. A family cannot print dollar bills (not legally, anyway), impose taxes on their neighbors or borrow in their own homegrown currency in the same way the federal government. American families earn and spend dollars, but the federal government is the issuer of those dollars. That, in theory, gives the government more fiscal flexibility than the average household.

Incurring national debt, something the country has done since its inception, can help Uncle Sam pay for necessary services and investments, from national defense and Social Security to infrastructure, education and scientific research. But excessive borrowing can increase interest costs, compound inflationary pressure when the U.S. economy is already under stress and leave future generations of Americans with fewer options. The national debt now exceeds $40.2 trillion. As Satyajit Das, a former banker, wrote on MarketWatch recently, government debt, higher energy prices and trade wars all pose a threat to a rising stock market.

Amen to the pastor's message. For those who did not read the letter you cite, a retired pastor wrote to The Moneyist to report that he had retired comfortably after earning $30,000 a year for most of his working life. His wife, a stay-at-home mom and homemaker, earned around $13,000 a year working in local schools. The pastor did not say whether he benefited from living in a grace-and-favor parsonage. That would have been a major expense to escape, and he would not have needed the services of a loan officer.

Related: 'I'd rather be on a beach in Bali': My husband resents my $8 million net worth. Should I pay for his retirement?

Reasons mortgages are denied

He, in turn, was responding to a letter from yet another reader (I'm 77, pay rent and live off Social Security, but I help homeless people), a retired senior citizen who reported that he was living month to month from his Social Security income - that is, he was getting by on modest means. After he paid his rent and bought his groceries and put money aside for his utilities, he said that he still found the resources to help homeless people. "Nobody should have to go without food in this country," he wrote.

According to data from 4,768 banks, credit unions and mortgage companies, 18% of mortgage applications were denied in 2025. That's based on figures released under the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act, from the Federal Financial Institutions Examination Council and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. Specifically, 929,064 out of 5.2 million applications were denied. The rejection rate was closer to 30% during the 2008-09 recession. For a prospective home buyer, it's one thing to get outbid - it's quite another being given a red card by your lender.

Some 18% of mortgage applications were denied last year, far lower than the 30% during the 2008-09 recession.

A 2025 report by the American Credit Union Mortgage Association, a national nonprofit trade group, delved into these application figures and concluded that credit unions reported significantly lower denial rates than other lenders. In 2025, credit unions had a denial rate of just over 18%, in part due to stronger member guidance through the qualification process, compared with roughly 32% for banks and 49.6% for independent mortgage brokers, with analysts pointing to strict loan-to-value limits and tough bank and consumer-protection regulations.

Sure, some people overspend and perhaps are destined to remain renters (at least for now), while other prospective homebuyers have their applications denied for more surprising reasons, some of which they can address. Wells Fargo outlines the most common reasons a mortgage application may be declined, such as a low credit score, high debt-to-income ratio (your original point), insufficient income, a property value that doesn't support the requested loan amount or an employment history that is either too short or inconsistent.

Looking to buy? The more feedback you get from the lender, the better. "There is no 'magic score' to qualify for a home mortgage, but a high score may qualify you for a higher loan or better interest rate," Wells Fargo says. "If you're interested in improving your credit score, you can take steps like paying your bills on time, keeping a low balance on your credit card and not applying for new credit. Continuing to build your financial literacy and learning about all the ways you can improve your financial situation could help you qualify for a loan in the future."

Income and debt are only part of the answer. Save more, spend less and invest the rest.

Related: I'm 71 and still working. I earn $108,000 a year. Am I doing the right thing?
